items.title: Leadership Summit 2026: Mattel’s CEO on Driving Consumer Engagement and Cultural Impact
items.summary: How do you reinvent an 80-year-old company without losing what made it successful in the first place? In this special episode, as part of the recent HBR Leadership Summit 2026, Mattel CEO Ynon Kreiz explains how he transformed the iconic toy maker into an IP-driven entertainment company that creates movies, games, live experiences, and digital products alongside its toys. He shares how simplifying strategy, reshaping talent, and fostering a culture of innovation helped drive the company's turnaround, why AI is accelerating product development without replacing creativity, and what leaders can learn about managing change, protecting trusted brands, and building organizations that are ready for the future.
items.claude_summary: Mattel CEO Ynon Kreiz describes how he repositioned an 80-year-old toy company into an IP-driven entertainment business spanning films, games, live experiences, and digital products. The conversation covers how strategic simplification, talent reshaping, and a deliberate culture of innovation underpinned the turnaround. On AI, Kreiz argues that the technology is accelerating product development cycles without displacing creative work. The episode is drawn from the HBR Leadership Summit 2026 and is based on a podcast interview rather than original research. The AI-related content appears limited to brief commentary, making it a general leadership story with a peripheral AI dimension.
items.centre_angle: This podcast interview argues that AI can compress product development timelines in a legacy consumer brand without eroding the creative work that defines the brand's identity. From CAMO's perspective on AI adoption, the more substantive organisational question is whether accelerating execution through AI reshapes job boundaries and managerial roles in ways leaders like Kreiz are not yet measuring — a dynamic explored in CAMO's nano-case on KFC China, where AI freed managerial attention for judgment-intensive work only after deliberate workflow redesign. The Mattel account, based on a single executive's self-reported view rather than systematic evidence, does not yet engage with that harder question.

matched_camo.title: Scaling Managers with AI at KFC China
matched_camo.reason: Both cases involve AI accelerating routine operational work in a large consumer-facing organisation, raising parallel questions about how managerial roles and creative capacity are redistributed rather than simply preserved.

items.key_takeaway: AI can speed up product development in established consumer brands, but the organisational implications for creative roles and managerial structure require more deliberate attention than a single executive's optimism suggests.

items.title: The Real Question to Ask About AI Governance
items.authors:
Joseph Wallace.

Joseph Wallace is the director of data and AI governance at Adobe, where he founded the enterprise governance program.
items.summary: Carolyn Geason-Beissel/MIT SMR | Getty Images Leaders at literally every Fortune 500 company will tell you that they are governing their AI — every single one of them. Now ask those same leaders who’s responsible for shutting down an AI model that’s causing harm. Most people can’t answer that question. That silence is the most […]
items.claude_summary: Most Fortune 500 companies claim to govern their AI, yet few leaders can name who is actually responsible for shutting down a harmful model. The article, written by Adobe's director of AI governance, argues that the operative question in AI governance is not 'are we governing AI?' but 'who has the authority and obligation to act when something goes wrong?' Without a clear accountability owner, governance frameworks become procedural theater — policies exist on paper while no individual bears real consequence for inaction. The piece makes the case that accountability assignment, not policy documentation, is the foundational design problem in enterprise AI governance.
items.centre_angle: This article argues that AI governance fails not from a lack of policy but from unresolved accountability — no one owns the decision to stop a harmful model. From CAMO's perspective on AI adoption inside organizations, this maps directly onto a structural problem: firms race to deploy AI while leaving authority structures ambiguous. CAMO's Deloitte-HKU AI Adoption Index found that the dominant barriers to successful AI adoption are organizational and executional rather than technical, and the absence of a named accountability owner is precisely the kind of executional gap that converts promising deployments into liability exposure. The article's framing complements CAMO's broader finding that closing the gap between AI promise and organizational performance requires deliberate redesign of roles and decision rights, not just investment in tools.

matched_camo.reason: Both identify organizational and executional gaps — siloed departments, cultural resistance, unclear ownership — as the primary obstacle to realizing AI value, not technical limitations.

matched_camo.reason: The MedTech case illustrates how poorly designed accountability structures around AI use produce perverse behavioral outcomes, directly echoing the article's argument that governance without real accountability owners is ineffective.

items.key_takeaway: AI governance is only as real as the named individual who can order a model shut down.

items.claude_summary: Anthropic's latest Economic Index report shifts focus from what Claude is used for to when and how people use it, sampling usage patterns hourly for the first time. The report asks three questions: at what points in the day do users turn to Claude, what outputs do they produce, and how do they themselves perceive AI's effect on their work? The excerpt is thin on specific findings, but the methodological move toward temporal sampling and self-reported perception data suggests the report is probing whether AI assistance is concentrated in particular workflow moments or distributed across the working day. This kind of usage-pattern data has direct implications for understanding how AI integrates into — or disrupts — existing work rhythms.
items.centre_angle: This report from Anthropic examines the temporal and perceptual texture of AI use at work — not just task categories, but when workers reach for AI and whether they believe it helps. From CAMO's perspective on AI adoption, this kind of cadence data is precisely what is missing from most enterprise adoption surveys: organisations measure access and output, rarely the moment-to-moment integration of AI into working routines. The self-perception component echoes a concern raised in CAMO's Deloitte-HKU AI Adoption Index 2026, where shallow adoption was identified even amid near-universal deployment — understanding when and why workers actually engage with AI tools is a prerequisite for moving beyond that shallowness.

matched_camo.reason: Both pieces probe the gap between AI availability and genuine integration into work, with the Anthropic report's cadence and perception data complementing CAMO's finding that adoption is wide but shallow.
matched_camo.title: Deloitte-HKU AI Adoption Index 2026: The Paradox of Promise and Performance

items.key_takeaway: Knowing when workers turn to AI — and whether they think it helps — may matter more for adoption strategy than knowing which tasks they use it for.

items.title: The real future of work in healthcare
items.summary: Healthcare is in a productivity crisis that more hiring and more technology alone will not solve. The next era of care depends on making automation work through human–AI workflows.
items.claude_summary: Healthcare faces a structural productivity crisis that cannot be resolved by hiring more staff or deploying more technology in isolation. The McKinsey article argues the real opportunity lies in redesigning human–AI workflows so that automation genuinely changes how care is delivered, not just how fast individual tasks are completed. The piece points to the gap between AI's technical potential and its operational impact, suggesting that workflow integration and role redesign—not tool acquisition—are the binding constraints. The excerpt is brief; specific evidence and quantitative claims from the full article are not available for assessment.
items.centre_angle: This article argues that healthcare's productivity crisis will only be resolved by rethinking human–AI workflows, not by stacking technology on top of existing processes. From CAMO's perspective on AI adoption, this maps precisely to an organizational design problem: AI optimizes tasks, but it is coordination and role structure that determine system-level gains—a dynamic documented in CAMO's Decathlon China case, where coding efficiency rose 20–40% but overall delivery speed improved only 10–15% until coordination work itself was redesigned. The healthcare context adds urgency because misaligned workflows carry patient-safety stakes that go beyond the commercial costs of shallow adoption.

matched_camo.title: Compressing Coordination with AI at Decathlon China
matched_camo.reason: Both the article and the Decathlon case identify the same structural insight: AI-driven efficiency gains at the task level fail to translate into system-level productivity when coordination structures and workflow design are left unchanged.

matched_camo.title: Toward a Bad Job Economy: AI Adoption, Agency Costs, and Job Design
matched_camo.reason: If healthcare organizations respond to AI-enabled efficiency by restructuring roles downward rather than redesigning workflows upward, the job-design dynamics modelled in this paper—where AI raises the incentive cost of sustaining high-effort roles—become directly relevant.

items.key_takeaway: In healthcare, the bottleneck to AI-driven productivity is not the technology itself but the organizational work of redesigning how humans and AI share tasks and decisions.

items.title: Three Approaches to Measuring and Managing AI ROI
items.authors:
Mika Ruokonen and Paavo Ritala.

Mika Ruokonen is industry professor of AI in business at LUT University’s LUT Business School in Finland. Paavo Ritala is professor of strategy and innovation at LUT Business School, LUT University, Finland.
items.summary: Matt Harrison Clough/Ikon Images After several years of AI experiments and pilot initiatives, a crucial question remains open for most companies: How much of a return — and what kinds of returns — are we getting from all of this AI investment? To many executives, AI ROI still often feels more like art than science: […]
items.claude_summary: After years of AI pilots and experiments, most companies still lack a rigorous method for measuring what they actually get back from AI investment. This article by two LUT University strategy researchers argues that AI ROI cannot be captured by a single metric and proposes three distinct measurement approaches, each suited to different types of AI initiatives. The core problem they identify is that executives treat ROI measurement as intuitive rather than systematic—more judgment call than structured analysis. The article is practitioner-oriented and offers a framework for categorizing returns, though the RSS excerpt is thin and the full argument is behind a paywall, so the depth of empirical grounding is unclear.
items.centre_angle: This article addresses one of the most persistent execution failures in enterprise AI: the absence of a coherent framework for measuring returns. From CAMO's perspective on AI adoption, this matters because poor ROI measurement is itself an organizational problem, not a technical one. CAMO's Deloitte-HKU AI Adoption Index 2026 found that nearly half of C-suite executives reported AI initiatives fell short of expected ROI, and identified siloed departments and lack of quick wins—not technology—as the dominant barriers; a structured approach to categorizing and tracking returns could directly address why so many adoption efforts stall before scaling.

matched_camo.reason: CAMO's own C-suite survey documents precisely the ROI shortfall and organizational barriers that this article's measurement framework is designed to address.
matched_camo.title: Deloitte-HKU AI Adoption Index 2026: The Paradox of Promise and Performance

items.key_takeaway: Measuring AI ROI requires a deliberate, categorized framework—not intuition—and choosing the wrong measurement approach for a given initiative is a structural reason returns disappoint.

items.title: AI Upskilling at Scale: Bank of America’s Bernard Hampton
items.authors:
Sam Ransbotham.

Me, Myself, and AI is a podcast produced by MIT Sloan Management Review and hosted by Sam Ransbotham. It is engineered by David Lishansky and produced by Allison Ryder.

Sam Ransbotham is a professor in the information systems department at the Carroll School of Management at Boston College, as well as guest editor for MIT Sloan Management Review’s Artificial Intelligence and Business Strategy Big Ideas initiative.
items.summary: Today’s episode of the Me, Myself, and AI podcast, the final one of Season 13, explores how Bank of America is preparing a massive global workforce for an AI future through upskilling and reskilling. Bernard Hampton, head of the financial institution’s Academy, explains how the learning and development organization focuses on workforce agility and a […]
items.claude_summary: Bank of America's head of its internal Academy, Bernard Hampton, describes how the bank is building AI literacy and capability across a large global workforce through systematic upskilling and reskilling programmes. The episode focuses on how a major financial institution's learning and development function is being repositioned around workforce agility in the face of AI adoption. Hampton outlines the structural and cultural challenges of preparing tens of thousands of employees for shifting job requirements, and the Academy's role in translating AI strategy into day-to-day capability building. Note: this is a podcast episode summary drawn from a brief RSS excerpt; specific findings and data points are not available for review.
items.centre_angle: This podcast episode argues that large-scale AI upskilling requires a dedicated institutional apparatus—not ad hoc training—to achieve genuine workforce agility. From CAMO's perspective on AI and jobs, the more consequential question is whether upskilling programmes address the social and incentive dynamics that govern actual tool adoption, not just technical access. CAMO's survey of HR professionals (State of AI in HR, 2026) finds that organisations prioritising time liberation and reframing AI as an upskilling tool see better adoption outcomes, while CAMO's experimental work on the hidden competence penalty for AI use suggests that employee reluctance to adopt may be rooted in social risk, which no amount of technical training alone resolves.

matched_camo.reason: Both examine how organisations build AI capability in their workforce, with the CAMO survey specifically identifying upskilling as a strategic outcome of AI-driven time savings in HR functions.
matched_camo.title: The State of AI in HR: Balancing Efficiency and Strategy

matched_camo.reason: Bank of America's upskilling focus implicitly assumes employees will use AI once trained, but CAMO's finding that AI use carries a social competence penalty points to a structural barrier that workforce training programmes typically do not address.
matched_camo.title: Research: The Hidden Penalty of Using AI at Work

items.key_takeaway: Deploying a dedicated institutional learning infrastructure is necessary but not sufficient for AI adoption at scale—organisations must also confront the social and incentive barriers that determine whether employees actually use the tools they are trained on.

items.title: Agentic AI: What Leaders Wish They Knew Sooner
items.summary: As AI agents go beyond the hypothetical and enter actual workflows, many leaders see a gap between the promise and the reality. Are the agents ready? Moreover, are the humans? At the 2026 MIT Sloan CIO Symposium, we sought expert perspective and advice. We asked technology and business leaders, “What have you learned this year […]
items.claude_summary: At the 2026 MIT Sloan CIO Symposium, technology and business leaders were asked what they have learned this year about deploying agentic AI in real workflows. The consistent theme, based on the excerpt, is a gap between expectation and reality: agents are entering production environments faster than the organizational and human readiness to absorb them. Leaders reflect on what they wish they had understood sooner about agentic AI — suggesting that the friction is less about the technology itself and more about how organizations, processes, and people adapt to systems that act autonomously on their behalf. The excerpt is brief and the full content is video-based, so specific findings cannot be confirmed.
items.centre_angle: This practitioner roundup from the 2026 MIT Sloan CIO Symposium surfaces a pattern CAMO's research consistently identifies: AI deployment outpaces organizational readiness, and the bottleneck is rarely technical. From CAMO's perspective on AI adoption, the 'promise versus reality' gap leaders describe mirrors what the Deloitte-HKU AI Adoption Index 2026 found among C-suite executives in China and Hong Kong — nearly half reported initiatives fell short of expected ROI, with siloed departments and cultural resistance as the dominant barriers. The agentic context sharpens this problem: when AI systems act autonomously rather than assist, the cost of misaligned incentives, unclear accountability, and unprepared workflows compounds quickly.

matched_camo.reason: Both pieces center on the gap between AI's anticipated impact and measurable organizational outcomes, with C-suite leaders as the primary voice on what impedes real deployment.
matched_camo.title: Deloitte-HKU AI Adoption Index 2026: The Paradox of Promise and Performance

matched_camo.reason: The Decathlon case illustrates concretely how agentic or multi-agent systems expose coordination bottlenecks that task-level AI cannot resolve — directly relevant to what leaders describe as readiness gaps in agentic workflows.
matched_camo.title: Compressing Coordination with AI at Decathlon China

items.key_takeaway: Agentic AI is entering real workflows faster than most organizations have prepared their people, processes, and accountability structures to handle it.
